citations.short_gloss: Earliest English provincial glossary witness of the goyster/gauster/goster ('to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud') verb family (< ME galstren).
citations.source_publication: Ray, John, A Collection of English Words Not Generally Used, with their Significations and Original, in two Alphabetical Catalogues, 1st ed. (London: Printed by H. Bruges for Tho. Barrell, 1674), p. 67.
citations.page_and_column: Title leaf n0 ('1674'); South and East Countrey Words, p. 67 (leaf n80)
citations.verbatim_quote: Gods good: Yeaſt, Barm. Kent, Norf. Suff. To Goyſter: to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud, Suff. Gowts, Somerſets. Canales, cloacæ, ſeu ſentinæ ſubterraneæ.
citations.linguistic_note: Establishes the seventeenth-century English dialectal verb stem underlying later northern and Midland gauster/goster (consonant skeleton KSTL, matching the second constituent of snollygoster with zero consonant-skeleton edit distance). In subsequent editions of Ray's Collection (including the 1737 third edition, North Country Words, p. 32), the northern vocalism is explicitly cross-referenced as 'To Gauſter; as Goyſter', descending from Middle English galstren ('to make a boisterous noise, cry out') with regular pre-sibilant l-vocalization.
citations.analysis_notes: Red-Team blind scan verified on John Ray's 1674 first-edition London title leaf (n0, 'Printed by H. Bruges for Tho. Barrell ... 1674') and p. 67 physical ink (leaf n80). Patched Pass 1's punctuation in verbatim_quote from 'laugh aloud. Suff.' to the printed comma 'To Goyſter: to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud, Suff.' (preserving long-s 'ſ') and uploaded an unclipped corrective WebP scan. MCP phonological scoring confirms goyster (consonant skeleton KWSTL) is chronologically plausible more than a century and a half prior to the 1845 American debut of 'Snolly Goster', representing the southern/East Anglian diphthongal sibling of northern gauster/goster (KSTL).

citations.short_gloss: South Yorkshire (Sheffield/Hallamshire) monophthongal spelling 'GOSTER' ('to boast, to bully, to hector') sixteen years prior to 1845 'Snolly Goster'.
citations.source_publication: Hunter, Joseph, The Hallamshire Glossary (London: William Pickering, 1829), p. 45.

citations.linguistic_note: Decisive orthographic and phonological donor witness: Hunter records the exact <o>-spelled form goster (/ˈɡɒstə(r)/, consonant skeleton KSTL) in South Yorkshire with the three-verb gloss 'to boast, to bully, to hector'. Under MCP phonological scoring against full compound snollygoster (SNLWKSTL), standalone goster naturally registers a four-consonant prefix gap before snolly- (SNLW) is attached, whereas as the right-hand compound head it matches -goster letter-for-letter and phoneme-for-phoneme.
citations.analysis_notes: Red-Team blind scan audit verified William Pickering's 1829 first-edition title leaf ('MDCCCXXIX.', leaf n6) and p. 45 physical ink (leaf n76), patching Pass 1's normalized terminal period to the 1829 compositor's actual printed comma at the close of the entry ('such a profanation of it,'). MCP phonological scoring confirms standalone goster (1829, skeleton KSTL) is chronologically plausible sixteen years before 1845 'Snolly Goster' and matches the four-consonant second element -goster of snollygoster (SNLWKSTL) exactly (leaving only the four-consonant first element SNLW- outside the simplex verb) while delivering the exact '<o>' spelling and 'boast, bully, hector' semantics echoed in 1841 Ohio Valley 'goster'.
